title: Synthetic staggered fields switch Neel vectors probed by magnetic resonance
authors: Yifang Hao, Zhiyi Che, Jack Brierley, Aakanksha Sud, Satoshi Iihama, Rishi Siddani, Chenghao Yang, Charlie W. F. Freeman, Troy Dion, Daniel Prestwood, Zekun Xue, Tianyi Wei, Murat Cubukcu, Craig Barton, Shunsuke Fukami, Shigemi Mizukami, Hidekazu Kurebayashi
abstract: Electrical detection of antiferromagnetic order is a critical challenge for antiferromagnetic spintronics owing to their vanishing macroscopic magnetisation. While magnetic resonance has demonstrated sub-terahertz antiferromagnetic spin pumping and nonlinear magnon dynamics, its application to electrically contacted on-chip devices has room for further exploration. Here we show that magnetic resonance enables direct electrical detection of Néel vector states. A $180^\circ$ reversal in synthetic antiferromagnets is realised by current-driven effective fields with opposite polarisation acting on each magnetic sublayer, which we term synthetic staggered fields. The switching induces a $π$ phase shift of precessional motion in time, producing hysteretic rectified voltages in our phase-sensitive detection scheme. Angular-dependent resonance analysis offers further insight into the Néel vector directions, pointing to a model beyond the macrospin formalism. We address this by defect-incorporated micromagnetic simulations that reveal fragmented domain states after current excitation. An extracted current density of $7.4\times10^{9}$ A/m$^2$ is, to our knowledge, the lowest reported value for the room-temperature Néel vector switching and we show that it scales with the in-plane uniaxial anisotropy both experimentally and numerically. Synthetic staggered fields and the resonance-based methodology provide a research platform for nanoscale characterisation of electrically driven antiferromagnetic textures, guiding the development of high-frequency on-chip spintronic architectures.
summary: This work presents a novel method to electrically detect and characterize the switching of Néel vector states in antiferromagnets using Spin-Torque Ferromagnetic Resonance. By applying synthetic staggered fields, the authors induce a measurable, hysteretic voltage signal proportional to the Néel vector reversal. This technique offers a powerful platform for developing high-frequency, on-chip spintronic devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the electrical detection of antiferromagnetic (AFM) order, which is difficult due to the vanishing macroscopic magnetization of AFM materials.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that magnetic resonance, utilizing synthetic staggered fields, enables direct electrical detection of Néel vector states, achieving record-low switching current densities.
method: The study combines electrical measurements (Spin-Torque Ferromagnetic Resonance, ST-FMR) with advanced micromagnetic simulations to characterize the switching mechanism.
model_or_system: The physical system involves synthetic antiferromagnets realized in multilayer thin films (e.g., Ta/NiFe/Ru/NiFe/Ta). The model incorporates current-driven effective fields (synthetic staggered fields) and accounts for defect-incorporated domain states beyond simple macrospin approximations.
key_observables: Hysteretic rectified voltages ($V_{dc}$), the anti-symmetric component of the resonance signal ($V_{asy}$), and spatially resolved vector stray fields ($\mathbf{B}_{\perp}, \mathbf{B}_{\parallel}, B_z$).
important_parameters: The critical current density ($J_c$) for Néel vector switching, which is shown to scale with in-plane uniaxial anisotropy, and the required current density ($7.4 	imes 10^9 	ext{ A/m}^2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a 1 nm top oxidation layer for current density calculations, and the initial theoretical framework uses the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of the setup, ST-FMR spectra showing $V_{dc}$ vs. $B$ and $I_{dc}$ with hysteresis, and simulations mapping the spatial distribution of magnetic stray fields ($\mathbf{B}_{\perp}, \mathbf{B}_{\parallel}, B_z$) before and after current pulsing.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the difficulty of AFM detection to demonstrating the measurement technique using ST-FMR, analyzing the switching mechanism via hysteresis and angular dependence, and finally validating the findings through advanced simulations and scaling studies.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter spintronics, the use of non-equilibrium current-driven dynamics to probe subtle magnetic textures (Néel vector) and the development of a highly sensitive, electrical detection method are relevant to understanding energy dissipation and non-linear dynamics in quantum systems.
